Of the ₹28,755 to ₹30,213 crore Jio Platforms raises, up to ₹27,500 crore repays borrowings, leaving ₹1,255 to ₹2,713 crore for everything else (BusinessLine).

Reliance is selling about 3% of Jio to clean its subsidiary's balance sheet, and it is pricing the sale to move: Uday Kotak of the lead bank said plainly, "We priced for investors to have returns in this IPO." That is smart treasury work, and the anchor queue of sovereign funds is the market's answer on demand.
But it means the growth story buyers are paying for, Akash Ambani's voice-AI bet, is funded by faith, not by this money.
My confidence: high on the arithmetic, because the RHP is filed and the filing is public; lower on how the market will price that AI optionality against ARPU that has been flat for two quarters.
What would prove me wrong: an anchor book on Monday that fills overwhelmingly at the ₹1,119 cap, which would show institutions are paying for the story, not the discount.

Jio Platforms Ltd (the telecom and digital arm of Reliance Industries) set a price band of ₹1,065 to ₹1,119 a share on Wednesday for an initial public offering (a first sale of shares to the public) of 27 crore fresh shares, opening 21 October and closing 23 October.
Employees get a ₹54 discount, the lot size is 12 shares (₹13,428 at the cap), and the face value is ₹10, all from Reliance's own exchange filing.
Three things sit inside that pricing.
First, it is entirely a fresh issue: no existing investor, not Meta, Google, KKR, Silver Lake or General Atlantic, is selling a share.
Second, the money mostly goes to lenders: the company carries borrowings of about ₹27,500 crore, so repayment leaves only ₹1,255 to ₹2,713 crore for general purposes (BusinessLine).
Deven Choksey of DRChoksey FinServ estimates the deleveraging cuts annual interest costs by ₹2,000 to ₹2,500 crore.

Third, demand is already visible: Mint reports ADIA, QIA, GIC, Norges Bank, Mubadala, BlackRock, FMR, Goldman Sachs Asset Management and Franklin Templeton, plus about 15 domestic asset managers, are seeking slots in an anchor book of about ₹8,000 crore, citing four people familiar with the plans.
The risk the roadshow kept circling is ARPU (average revenue per user, the monthly bill per subscriber): it rose to ₹215.6 from ₹214 across a year, and was flat the quarter before.

Managing director Akash Ambani's answer: realisation per user can grow outside licensed services, "one key example being our voice AI service." The company reported a profit of ₹30,064 crore on revenue of ₹1.49 lakh crore in FY26.
Reserved quotas: ₹2,500 crore for Reliance shareholders and ₹500 crore for employees.
Why it matters to you: The pricing tells you what the seller thinks the market will pay, not what the business is worth.
Kotak said the band was set from roadshow feedback so investors make money.
If that intent is real, Monday's anchor book fills near the ₹1,119 cap; if it fills near the ₹1,065 floor, the discount was demanded by buyers, not offered by the seller.
The chart shows sector index moves only, 12 of 23 NSE sectoral indices.
IT led at +3.92% and Capital Markets lagged at -1.07%; 14 of 23 rose.
Over the past five sessions the Nifty IT index is up 11.72%, the strongest weekly move of any sector.
A sector index moving shows the average stock in it moved; it is not by itself proof of money rotating between sectors.
Flows: foreign institutional investors bought ₹1,165.92 crore on Friday, returning after a selling stretch, while domestic institutional investors sold ₹3,661.28 crore (CNBC-TV18).
The rupee closed at 94.95 per dollar and Brent at $109.86 a barrel; both matter for Monday because oil is India's largest import bill and IT earns in dollars.

Largest IPO in India's history.

Why it matters to you: Worth a closer look if you planned to apply for one large listing this year: the anchor queue and a band set below street estimates give the issue visible support.
The case weakens if Monday's anchor book fills near the ₹1,065 floor instead of the cap, or if grey market premiums collapse after the anchor names are public.
Paras Healthcare runs eight hospitals across Patna, Darbhanga, Gurugram, Panchkula, Udaipur, Ranchi, Kanpur and Srinagar.

The issue: ₹660 to ₹693 a share, lot of 21, a fresh issue of 71.15 lakh shares (₹500 crore) plus an offer for sale (OFS, existing shareholders selling their shares) of 1.37 crore shares (₹950 crore) by promoter Dr Dharminder Kumar Nagar and Commelina.
Fresh proceeds go to repaying debt at the company and its subsidiary PMHPL, and general purposes.

Grey market premium stands at ₹95 per share, 13.71% above the cap, implying an estimated listing price of ₹788, as of 9:37 pm on 16 October (investorgain.com); unofficial grey market data, steady over the last three sessions, shown as sentiment.
Why it matters to you: Worth a closer look only if you are comfortable with regional hospital chains.

The case weakens on the structure: ₹950 crore of the ₹1,450 crore issue is promoters selling, and the fresh ₹500 crore goes to repay debt, so listing-day buyers fund an exit and a balance sheet, not new beds.

Also listing this week (Upstox): HD Fire Protect and Vaibhav Vyapaar on Tuesday 21 October; Fusion CX and Ravita Engineering Services on Wednesday 22; Sahajanand Medical Technologies, Tonbo Imaging, Bonfiglioli Transmissions, Zetwerk and Shellz India on Thursday 23.
Indian startups raised $231.5 million across 26 rounds this week, more than double the previous week and down 45.3% from a year ago (Tracxn data via ETtech).

The four largest: Boldfit, the fitness brand, ₹400 crore; GreenCell Mobility, the electric bus operator, ₹330 crore led by Impact Fund Denmark; Scimplify, a specialty chemicals sourcing platform, $25 million led by Hitachi Ventures; Nat Habit, an ayurvedic personal care brand, ₹142 crore.
Why it matters to you: The week-on-week doubling is a base effect after a slow week; the year-on-year drop of 45.3% is the structural number.
Seed and early-stage cheques keep flowing while late-stage stays scarce, which is what a valuation-reset market looks like.
Every red herring prospectus states what the money will do; almost nobody checks twelve months later.
Build a tracker that reads RHPs, extracts the stated use of proceeds, and scores each company's annual report against its own promise.
Buyers: institutional research desks, IPO-focused retail platforms, and the anchor desks themselves.
Why now: a record pipeline means a record pile of promises.
What breaks it: ministry filings are messy to parse, and "general corporate purposes" is designed to be untrackable, so the product has to score honesty about vagueness too.
Why it matters to you: Jio's own raise shows the gap: 91% of India's largest IPO goes to lenders, while the roadshow sells an AI story.
A promises-versus-delivery scoreboard would price that gap across every listing, and anchor investors and analysts would pay for it.

In August 1970, the Quarterly Journal of Economics published "The Market for Lemons: Quality Uncertainty and the Market Mechanism" by George Akerlof, then fresh from a year at the Indian Statistical Institute in Delhi, which the paper thanks.
It won him a share of the 2001 Nobel Prize.
The setup: a used-car market where sellers know which cars are lemons and buyers do not.
Buyers therefore pay only the average price.
Sellers of good cars refuse to sell at the average price and leave.
The average quality falls, so buyers lower their price again, and the market unwinds until only lemons trade.
Akerlof's own insurance example is the sharpest part of the paper.
People over 65 struggle to buy health insurance at any price: as premiums rise to cover the riskiest applicants, healthier seniors drop out, and the pool gets sicker.
He noted group insurance through employers fixes this by pooling the healthy and the sick together.

His larger point: when information is asymmetric, markets do not just price badly, they can fail to exist, and institutions such as guarantees, brand names and licensing arise precisely to keep them alive.
The line to carry into Monday: IRDAI's lapse problem is the same machine running in reverse.
A policyholder who surrenders tells the insurer something the insurer prices against; a loan against surrender value is an attempt to keep the good risks in the pool.
Whether it works depends on the loan's price, which is why Seth flagged exactly that.
Closed-book test: 1) Why do sellers of good used cars leave a market where buyers cannot verify quality?
2) Why does employer group insurance resist the lemons spiral better than individual senior-citizen policies?
3) Name two countervailing institutions Akerlof lists.
Answers: 1) They refuse the average price, which prices their car as if it were a lemon.
2) The pool is assembled for a reason other than insurance, so the healthy cannot self-select out.
3) Guarantees and brand names (licensing is the third).
Why it matters to you: Insurance exists inside this problem.
An insurer cannot tell a healthy 40-year-old from a sick one at the same price, so it prices for the average, the healthy leave, prices rise, and more healthy leave.
Every institution in your industry, medical tests, waiting periods, group policies, is a countervailing institution of exactly the kind Akerlof listed.

Today's long read is the story of Zerodha: a 17-year-old trader, two busts, four years on a call-centre night shift, and a broking licence bought with crash savings, which built India's second-largest broker by active clients without a rupee of outside money or advertising, and which now faces the regulator ending the weekly-options trade that made it.
It ends on the decision the founders themselves say is on the table: charging for delivery trades for the first time.
Read it here: Zerodha: built without a rupee of outside money (about 20 minutes).
